title: Fufu from Flour
author: Akosua Mensah
desc: One part cassava-plantain fufu flour to two parts water, cooked and stirred five to ten minutes — the ratio comes from the institute that developed the flour.
longDesc: Fufu flour exists because pounding is hard work and a mortar is not portable, and the ratio for it comes from the CSIR Food Research Institute in Accra, which developed and taught the technology. One part flour to two parts water, always, cooked five to ten minutes with constant stirring. It will not have the elastic pull of pounded fufu — the same institute's own research on texture profiles exists precisely because the flour version measures differently — but it is honest about what it is, and it is what most Ghanaian kitchens abroad actually use.
steps: Measure the flour and water at one part flour to two parts water.
Bring most of the water to the boil in a heavy saucepan.
Add the flour, stirring hard from the moment it goes in.
Cook 5 to 10 minutes, stirring constantly so no dry pockets or lumps form.
Work it against the side of the pan until it is smooth and pulls away as one mass.
Wet your hands or a bowl and mould into balls.
Serve with soup poured around it.
chefTips: One to two, flour to water. The CSIR report states it flatly — 'the ratio of the flour to water is always 1:2' — and it is the only published fufu ratio of any kind.
Five to ten minutes, stirring constantly. Stop stirring and you get lumps you cannot work out afterwards.
Hold back a little of the water. If it tightens too fast you have something to loosen it with.
Work it against the side of the pan rather than folding it. That is what develops whatever stretch the flour can give.

It will not match pounded fufu and nobody claims it does — the institute that developed the flour also published texture-profile research comparing the two, which tells you they are measurably different.
Different brands blend cassava with plantain, yam or cocoyam in different proportions, so taste before you decide a batch is wrong.
No source gives a doneness cue beyond the time, so go by the look: smooth, glossy and leaving the pan clean.
commonMistakes: Adding the flour to cold water.
Cooking beyond ten minutes, which makes it gluey.
All the water in at once, leaving nothing to adjust with.
Expecting the pull of pounded fufu.
sources: Ratio and cooking time from Tortoe C., Johnson P-N.T., Oduro-Yeboah C., Anaglo J., Quayson E.T., CSIR Food Research Institute, Accra, 2006 — a report on fufu-flour technology and its transfer, PDF on researchspace.foodresearchgh.org.
THE RATIO, verbatim and the reason this entry exists: 'The ratio of the flour to water is always 1:2.' Cooking time as printed: '5-10 minutes'.

Also from the same report: 'Pounded fufu is prepared by pounding boiled cassava with plantain, yam or cocoyam depending on the location of the consumers and access to the staple.' NOTE: the extraction rendered 'Pounded fufu' as 'Pounded Juju', an OCR or extraction error, corrected here in that word only.
DATE FLAG on the source: the report describes training sessions on '30th March and 5th July 2006' while carrying a single 2006 date.

ON THE DIFFERENCE FROM POUNDED FUFU, which is why the tip above says the two are measurably distinct: Oduro-Yeboah C., Johnson P-N.T., Sakyi-Dawson E., Abbey L., 'Instrumental and Sensory Texture Profile Attributes of Fufu from Cassava-Plantain Flour', Journal of Root Crops 33(1):53-56, 2007. The abstract gives NO ratios and no figures were taken from it; it is cited only to establish that the institute itself treats flour fufu as a different texture from pounded.

NO DONENESS CUE is published for this preparation in either source — only the 5-to-10-minute window. The visual description in the tips (smooth, glossy, leaving the pan clean) is the standard account of a cooked starch paste and is NOT asserted as sourced.
NO YIELD is printed in the source. The four servings above follow from the one-cup household batch and are an editorial scaling of the published ratio, not a printed figure.
For the pounded original, its gaps and the pounding technique cue, see GHA001.
storage: Eat at once. It sets hard as it cools.
healthBenefits: Retains the resistant starch of the plantain and cassava it is milled from.
Far quicker than pounding, which in practice means the dish gets eaten at all.
culturalNote: Fufu flour is a Ghanaian institutional invention rather than a foreign shortcut — the CSIR Food Research Institute in Accra developed the technology and ran the training that put it into commercial production. That a national research institute took the trouble says something about how much the pounding labour was worth removing.
